concept: Programs break: a bug is a mistake in a program
alt: The Debug Lab opens a program that does not work: Bolt waits at the start while the broken program fills the tray.

concept: Expected and actual: compare what Bolt did with what you expected
alt: Bolt has run part of the broken program and stopped in the wrong place: what Bolt did is not what the program promised.

concept: Step, stop, fix: step one block at a time and stop at the first surprise
alt: Stepping one block at a time: the first block is lit in the tray and Bolt has moved exactly one square.

concept: One too many: a repeat count one too big is a common bug
alt: The broken program is one repeat block set to 6, but the flag is five squares away: one move too many.

actions.program: move; move; move; right; move; move; move

concept: Done means tested: a fix is done when you run it again
alt: The fixed program sits in the tray: the wrong turn left has become turn right, ready to run again and be tested.

concept: Expect bugs: a test case is one board with a known right answer
alt: A Pro Debug Lab board with its test tabs above it: one program must pass every board, not just this one.

actions.program: repeat 5 { move }; left; repeat until goal { move }

concept: One board can hide a bug: the same program on a second test board
alt: The same program on Test 3, a longer hallway: Test 1 and Test 2 show a check, Test 3 a cross, and Bolt splashed into the water.

concept: Edge cases: unusual boards break quiet assumptions
alt: A later Debug Lab board with an unusual layout: goals and walls sit where a program that assumes too much will fail.

actions.program: repeat 5 { move }; left; repeat until goal { move }

concept: The debug loop: a fix is done only when every test passes
alt: After a run, every test tab shows a mark: Test 1 and Test 2 pass, Test 3 fails, so this fix is not done yet.

concept: Be the game designer: plan, build, test, fix, explain
alt: The Level Maker's first task: the goal is walled in, and the floor and wall tools wait beside the board.

concept: Plan it first: start, goal and one tricky part
alt: A second maker task brief on the canvas: each task says what the level must contain before a single square is painted.

concept: The maker loop: Check proves a level can be solved and shows its par
alt: A level built in the maker: Bolt, a gem, a key, a door and the goal on the board, and Check says it can be solved: par 17.

concept: The designer stays quiet: a tester plays while the designer watches
alt: The built level handed to a tester: the tester builds a program and Bolt drives it, while the maker watches without helping.

concept: Design for someone else: plan, build, test, improve, document
alt: The Pro Level Maker's first task: the goal is walled in, and the tools to open the walls wait beside the board.

concept: Keep a timeline: split the work and set times
alt: A second Pro maker task: the brief sets what to build, the way a team plan sets who does each part and by when.

concept: Iterate: plan, build, Check, test, change, test again
alt: A Pro maker level with a gem, a key and a door on the way to the goal, and Check says it can be solved: par 23.

actions.program: move; move; move; move; move; right; move; move; right; move; move; move; move; move; left; move

concept: Feedback is information: it shows where a player got stuck
alt: After a friend tests the level, the tester card asks for one fun thing and one confusing thing, with nothing to type.

concept: Meet Dot: a detective solves cases with facts, not guesses
alt: Dot opens the first case: a table of who, where and when facts in rows and columns, and the question: who was last in the hall?

concept: Data is facts in rows: a table holds facts in rows and columns
alt: Another case table: every row is one tower of blocks, every column one kind of fact about it.

concept: Sort or group: grouping puts the same kind together and counts them
alt: The pet case grouped: one bar per kind of pet, counted, so the most common pet jumps out of the chart.

concept: Who was in the lunchroom last? Sort by the column the question asks about
alt: The case sorted by time: the Hall rows now run in time order, so the last Hall row answers the question.

concept: Show me first: pin a claim only when the view on screen shows it
alt: With the grouped chart showing the evidence, the claim card opens: Dot will only pin a claim the view proves.

concept: Is it true? A claim is backed up by evidence
alt: The Plant Race case: a chart of a growing plant, and claim cards waiting to be judged against it.

concept: Enough data? Two bars are a hunch, not a case
alt: The Two Points case: a chart with almost no data in it, where the honest answer is that we can not tell yet.

concept: Predict the plant: it grows 2 cm every day
alt: Predict Day 6: the plant chart climbs the same amount every day, so the next bar can be predicted from the pattern.

concept: Say only what it shows: a chart does not say why
alt: The claim card beside the plant chart: each claim must match what the bars actually show, nothing more.

concept: Data from real people: today the data comes from people around you
alt: My Data opens a class survey: one question, and answer rows waiting for the class to fill them in.

concept: Tally marks: each answer gets one mark, counted in fives
alt: Tallying the survey: answers are counted with the steppers, each one adding to its row of the class data.

concept: From tally to chart: one bar per answer, the tallest jumps out
alt: The survey tallies turned into a bar chart: one bar per pet, and the dog bar towers over the rest.

concept: Ask someone else: another pair of eyes may see what you missed
alt: A second survey question waits in My Data: fresh answers to collect before anyone pins a claim about them.

concept: Real data is messy: typos, repeats and impossible numbers
alt: The Twelve Pets case as it arrived: a messy table where one kind of pet hides under several spellings.

concept: Clean it first: fix typos, merge repeats, remove impossible values
alt: Double Trouble: a second messy case, where the same student answered twice and one row must go.

concept: Pet survey clean-up: three spellings of dog split one bar into three
alt: The cleaned pet chart: the three misspelled dogs are fixed to one spelling, and the Dog bar counts all seven.

concept: Compare by percent: part divided by whole, times 100
alt: Tidy, Then Compare: two cleaned sets side by side, the case where comparing fairly means comparing percents.

concept: Rules that predict: a model is a rule, a simulation runs it
alt: The Ramp Rule case: a rule that predicts how far a car rolls, with the ramp and the trials waiting.

concept: Predict, compare, refine: change the model, not the data
alt: The model has run: predicted distances sit beside the real trials, so the rule can be compared and refined.

concept: The ramp: every trial went farther than predicted, so refine the rule
alt: The ramp trials ran farther than the first rule predicted, so the rule was raised and run again: the error shrinks.

concept: One trial is not proof: compare the model with many results
alt: Bounce Back: another model case with its own trials, because one lucky trial never proves a rule.

concept: Fair questions first: answers can only be fair if questions are fair
alt: My Data in Pro: a survey question and its answer rows, where fairness starts with how the question is asked.

concept: Leading questions: a question that pushes builds in bias
alt: A second Pro survey question: its wording matters, because a pushing question bends the data before counting.

concept: Fix the question: let every answer feel equally welcome
alt: One Grade Asked: a fairness case about who a survey asked, and who it never reached.

concept: A bigger, fairer sample: more answers from more kinds of people
alt: Who Is Missing? The fairness case that asks which people a sample left out before trusting its answer.

concept: Compare by percent: compare 72% with 50%, not 18 with 20
alt: A third survey question in My Data: the case for comparing classes by percent instead of raw counts.

concept: Meet Pim: every message must reach the right house
alt: Pim opens the Netville map: houses, roads and the first message waiting to be delivered.

concept: Too big to send: the network cuts a message into numbered packets
alt: Break It Up: a message too big for one trip is cut into small numbered packets at the post office.

concept: Back in order: numbers put arriving packets back together
alt: Packets are on the roads of Netville, each carrying its number, so the far end can rebuild the message in order.

concept: Many roads: each packet can take a different road through routers
alt: Many Roads: the town map offers more than one road between the same houses, and a closed road is not the end.

concept: Lock it up: lock it, keep the key, keep a spare copy
alt: The mailbox key builder: pick words for a passphrase, the key that locks your mailbox in Packet Post.

concept: Private or fine to share? Some things stay private
alt: The sharing sort: cards to split into Share and Keep Private, from favorite animals to passphrases.

concept: Build a passphrase: four random words, long and hard to guess
alt: The passphrase is taking shape: words are being picked for the mailbox key, and longer means harder to guess.

concept: Who may know it? Only a trusted adult may know your passphrase
alt: Okay to Tell: a sorting round about who may hear what, where a passphrase is never fine to share.

concept: Keep a spare copy: a backup kept somewhere else
alt: A Good Spare Copy: the sorting round that tells a real backup, kept somewhere else, from a copy that is not.

concept: Some messages are tricks: they want you to hurry or give things away
alt: Spot the Trick opens its first message card: friendly words on the surface, and clues hiding in the text.

concept: Clues of a trick: hurry, a prize, a request for your passphrase
alt: Checking the message: the first clue is marked, and the card still has more of its tricks to find.

concept: Trick or safe? A threat, a rush and a key request
alt: A second message card to judge: is it a trick with clues, or a safe message with none?

concept: What to do: do not reply, do not tap, tell a trusted adult
alt: A third trick card: the safe move is always the same — stop, do not reply, and tell a trusted adult.

concept: Secret codes for fun: a cipher wheel shifts each letter by the key (shift 3)
alt: The cipher wheel: turn the key and every letter shifts, turning a plain message into a secret one.

concept: Messages in packets: numbered, routed and rebuilt at the other end
alt: Rules of the Road opens: numbered packets wait at the first router, ready to travel by the shared rules.

concept: Rules everyone follows: a protocol is rules every computer agrees on
alt: A second protocol level: every router on the road follows the same rules, or no packet could be passed on.

concept: Say got it: the receiver confirms each packet and asks for missing ones
alt: The delivery is under way: packets have been sent and the receiver is saying got it, watching for a gap.

concept: Damaged on the way? A checksum count that does not match means resend
alt: A later protocol level on the road: here a damaged packet must be spotted by its count and sent again.

concept: Hops: each jump between routers is one hop, inside a hop budget
alt: Many Roads in Pro: the map counts hops, and a busy router means picking another path inside the budget.

concept: Two halves of security: physical protects the machine, digital the data
alt: Lock It in Pro opens with the sharing sort: security starts with knowing what must be protected.

concept: Physical or digital? Sort each measure by what it protects
alt: Physical or Digital: the sort whose bins are the machine and the data, from locked doors to firewalls.

concept: The padlock: details travel sealed, like an envelope, not a postcard
alt: The sealed route: a message travels a road marked sealed, the padlock idea played as a journey.

concept: Strong passphrases: four random words beat a short word plus a number
alt: The Pro mailbox key builder: a passphrase made of chosen words, different from every other account key.

concept: Think before you post: making something public has a benefit and a risk
alt: The last Lock It sort in Pro: judging what is safe to do, the habit of naming a risk before you act.

concept: Scramble it: encryption makes a message unreadable without the key
alt: Secret Messages in Pro: the cipher wheel waits with a scrambled message only the key can open.

concept: A shift of 3: every letter moves the same number of places
alt: The wheel at work: letters are shifting along the alphabet by the key, turning plain words into code.

concept: Brute force: a shift has only 25 keys, so you can try them all
alt: A later cipher level: with so few keys, trying every one is a real way in — for a shift cipher.

concept: Hiding is not scrambling: a found hidden message can be read at once
alt: Another cipher level on the wheel: scrambling with a key, which is stronger than merely hiding a message.

concept: Hiding is not scrambling: steganography hides a message in a picture's pixels
alt: Steganography: a heart hidden in a picture. Each pixel is a number, and its last bit says dot or blank, so the picture looks the same.

concept: Faked senders: a trick can fake its sender name, called spoofing
alt: A Pro trick card: the sender name looks friendly, but a faked name is exactly what spoofing means.

concept: Meet Gizmo: every device is a team of parts
alt: Gizmo opens the tablet: its parts are laid out as a team, and the first job asks which part does it.

concept: Every part has a job: inputs, outputs, processor, storage, battery
alt: Inside the machine: the cutaway view where the processor, storage and battery do their jobs together.

concept: A tap travels: finger, touch sensor, processor, the app, screen
alt: The controller pad wiring round: parts are joined in the order a signal travels from input to output.

concept: Hardware and software: hardware you can touch, software is instructions
alt: The hardware and software sort: cards for screens and apps wait to be split into touchable and instructions.

concept: Every task needs both: a photo needs the camera and the camera app
alt: An ordering round: the steps of one task laid out, where hardware and software take turns doing the work.

concept: It is not working! Good fixers have a plan, not a panic
alt: The Fix-It Desk opens its first ticket: a broken gadget, its story, and the fix options with their minutes.

concept: Quick checks first: on, plugged in, muted — restart comes later
alt: A second ticket waits at the desk: the quick, cheap checks are the ones a good fixer tries first.

concept: No sound: troubleshooting is a checklist, not a guess
alt: The No Sound ticket: the headphones fix is under way, with plugged in and volume checked on the list.

concept: Small clues: caps lock, a frozen app — the clue points at the fix
alt: A fourth ticket with a small clue in its story: reading the clue closely points straight at the fix.

concept: On or off: everything inside is tiny switches, called bits
alt: Five bit switches, all off, with their cards: 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1. One switch on adds its card.

concept: Make the number 5: turn on the switches that add up to 5
alt: The 4 card and the 1 card are switched on: 4 and 1 make 5, the number this round asked for.

concept: Counting with bits: read the cards whose switch is on
alt: A reading round: some switches are already on, and the question is what number their cards add up to.

concept: Pictures are dots: a picture is tiny dots called pixels
alt: The pixel grid: a picture drawn one dot at a time, each cell lit or dark like a bit.

concept: Where does a photo live? In storage, as bits, even when off
alt: The photo question: where is a photo when the tablet is off? The answer the game teaches is storage, as bits.

concept: A step counter: small, cheap, lasts all day — pick only what it needs
alt: The Step counter brief: a shoe clip that counts steps, small, cheap and lasting all day, with cost, battery and size meters.

concept: Sensors: a sensor measures the world — light, motion, sound
alt: A second gadget brief: choosing parts starts with the sensor that measures what the gadget must notice.

concept: Tradeoffs: every part costs money, battery and space
alt: A third brief with tighter limits: every part added moves the cost, battery and size meters.

concept: What makes a gadget: sensors, a processor, outputs, a connection and power
alt: A Noise meter brief: it must hear the room, show the loudness, send a log to the laptop and run on wall power.

concept: Fixers do not guess: a flowchart of yes/no questions, cheapest first
alt: The Pro Fix-It Desk opens a flow ticket: the fix is a chain of yes and no questions, cheapest first.

concept: One change at a time: change one thing, then test again
alt: A second Pro ticket: the flowchart way means one change, one test, and knowing what fixed it.

concept: The printer prints nothing: cheap checks before slow, expensive ones
alt: A third Pro ticket at the desk: its story hides the clue, and the cheap checks come before the slow ones.

concept: The swap test: swap in a part you know works and watch the problem
alt: A later Pro ticket: the kind where swapping in a known-good part tells you where the fault lives.

concept: Everything is numbers: letters and colors are bits too
alt: Pro bits opens with five switches and a bigger ask: make 21, where every place is worth double the last.

concept: Binary place values: each place is worth double the one to its right
alt: The color round: a swatch to match with three numbers, because a pixel mixes red, green and blue light.

concept: More bits, more values: eight bits, a byte, show 256 grays
alt: Eight switches in a row: a full byte, worth 0 to 255. Only the 128 switch is on, making the middle gray.

concept: One thing, many codes: 21 in decimal is 10101 in binary
alt: The switches read 16, 4 and 1 switched on: the number 21 written in bits instead of decimal.

concept: Made for everyone: a good game works for people who differ
alt: Design Lab opens with a user to design for: their needs come first, before any setting is touched.

concept: Help one, help many: captions help in a noisy room too
alt: A second Design Lab user: a change made for one person usually turns out to help many more.

concept: Every switch is for someone: captions, read-aloud, text size, contrast
alt: The audit round: a real game is checked setting by setting — captions, text size, contrast — for who each helps.

concept: Design for real people: start with how real people use a thing
alt: Design Lab in Pro opens with a real user and their words: design starts from what people actually say.

concept: Edges help everyone: contrast for low vision helps in bright sun too
alt: A Pro brief about designing at the edges: a mode made for low vision is the mode everyone uses in sun.

concept: Bias: tech works worse for some when testers were all alike
alt: A Pro brief about bias: when a product fails some people, the testing group is the first place to look.

concept: Who was missing? Find the gap in the testing group, then widen it
alt: The last Pro brief: find who was missing from the testers, then widen the group until nobody is.

concept: What is technology? Anything people invent to solve a problem
alt: A Would You Rather technology dilemma: two inventions to choose between, and reasons to weigh on both sides.

concept: Tech changes how we live: every invention changes something else
alt: A second technology dilemma: a new choice about how an invention changes the way people live.

concept: Tradeoffs everywhere: a benefit for someone, a cost for someone else
alt: A Pro technology dilemma: each side of the choice helps someone and costs someone else.

concept: Automation: a machine does a task people used to do
alt: Another technology dilemma, about machines doing tasks people used to do, and what changes when they do.

concept: Write a credit line / share or keep: weigh both sides before sharing
alt: A Would You Rather online dilemma: something you made, and the choice of whether to share it or keep it.

concept: Public or private? Public gets you seen, private keeps you safe
alt: An online dilemma in Pro: make it public and be found, or keep it private and stay safe — a real tradeoff.

concept: Post your art? Benefit: feedback. Risk: a logo shows where you are
alt: A second online dilemma: posting your work brings feedback, and can also show more than you meant.
